question.knowledge_point: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle
question.problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{5}{9}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{5}{9} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{4}{9} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{2}{3}.$

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931905/assets/52fe94bb303a001e89f9db221e9730d4ca8c5c284217aa20fb6084ee041dec66.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4})}^{2} \\  & =2-2(\frac{10}{16}) \\  & =2-\frac{20}{16} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So our final answer is $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931905/assets/f5219a363cdf18cfb628148ca7b9bbe6015b521799ed4487fa9b56843eaa3043.png)

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{6}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.$

Knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡\theta  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
